member.name: T:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Extensions.AbortAtDeadlineExtension
member.summary: Reacts to a CI-imposed hard-cancel deadline (see ): a short margin before the deadline it asks the test framework to gracefully stop scheduling new tests, so the in-flight session can end normally and all reporters (TRX/HTML/AzDO live run) get to finalize before the CI runner hard-kills the process.
member.remarks: This is a prototype. It is timer-driven (the deadline is an absolute instant, so the timer is armed at construction). It implements so the message bus keeps a live reference to it for the duration of the run (which also keeps its timer alive); it consumes no message types, so the bus keeps that reference without routing any message to it. It also implements as a backstop and is registered as a service so the host can call the moment the test framework invoker returns. That early signal prevents a timer firing while reporters finalize an already-finished run from marking it deadline-truncated.

member.name: F:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Extensions.AbortAtDeadlineExtension.DisposeDrainTimeout
member.summary: Bounded wait applied on disposal to let an in-flight deadline handler finish reporting before the host tears down, without letting a wedged stop hang disposal forever.

member.name: F:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Extensions.AbortAtDeadlineExtension.DefaultReportTimeout
member.summary: Bounded wait applied to each best-effort diagnostic on the deadline path, so a logger or output device that never completes cannot hold up the graceful stop it precedes.
member.remarks: Generous enough that a healthy provider never hits it, and short relative to the margin the deadline leaves for the stop to take effect.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Extensions.AbortAtDeadlineExtension.NotifyTestExecutionCompleted
member.summary: Disarms the deadline because test execution has finished.
member.remarks: The host calls this as soon as the test framework invoker returns, before end-of-session draining and reporting begin. That instant matters: from here on the deadline is moot, because every test that was going to run has run. Doing it through instead would be far too late -- session-end notification first drains the message bus, then runs the non-consumer handlers, then the consumer handlers in registration order, and this extension is a consumer appended after the reporters. A deadline reached anywhere in that window would still mark a fully-executed run as truncated (exit code 15). The transition is made under the same lock that claims the deadline, and only out of , so it is atomic against claiming the stop. Completion after the deadline claim is recorded separately so a rejected stop can restore the completed state without invoking framework code while holding the lock. The timer itself is left to be disposed at host teardown; the state is what makes any late fire a no-op.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Extensions.AbortAtDeadlineExtension.WaitForDeadlineHandlingAsync
member.summary: Waits until a deadline stop request that raced test-execution completion has resolved its verdict.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Extensions.AbortAtDeadlineExtension.TryClaimDeadline
member.summary: Atomically claims the deadline while test execution is still running.
member.remarks: Framework code is invoked only after releasing the lock. Completion that occurs after the claim is tracked by and reconciled if the stop is rejected.

member.name: T:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Extensions.AbortAtDeadlineExtension.RunState
member.summary: Which of test execution finishing and the deadline firing took the run. The winner is claimed only out of and under the extension's lock; completion during a deadline claim is recorded separately so a rejected stop can restore the completed state.

member.name: F:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Extensions.AbortAtDeadlineExtension.RunState.Running
member.summary: Test execution is in progress, so the deadline still applies.

member.name: F:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Extensions.AbortAtDeadlineExtension.RunState.Completed
member.summary: The test framework invoker returned: every test that was going to run has run, so a deadline reached from here on must not mark the run as truncated.

member.name: F:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Extensions.AbortAtDeadlineExtension.RunState.DeadlineClaimed
member.summary: The deadline fired while tests were still running and owns the verdict. Test execution completing afterwards is the stop taking effect, so it must not take the verdict back.

member.name: F:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Extensions.AbortAtDeadlineExtension.RunState.DeadlineClaimedAndCompleted
member.summary: Test execution completed after the deadline claim but before the framework accepted the stop. If the framework rejects the stop, the run returns to rather than .

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Extensions.AbortAtDeadlineExtension.TryReportAsync(System.Func{System.Threading.Tasks.Task},System.String)
member.summary: Runs a best-effort diagnostic, swallowing anything it throws and giving up on it if it does not complete promptly, so it can never skip or delay the graceful stop.

member.summary: Gets the lowercase file extensions, including the leading dot, used to match artifacts produced by older hosts that do not provide a kind.
Processes matching artifacts and writes at most one result under .
member.param: The input artifacts. Implementations must treat them as read-only.
The directory under which the processed artifact must be written.
The context describing the test run that produced the artifacts.
member.returns: The processed artifact representing all , or when no processing is needed.
member.remarks: Implementations must be deterministic and idempotent because orchestrators may retry transient failures. A non- result must represent every supplied input. Implementations that cannot produce one artifact representing the complete input set must return or throw. When a processor declares both kinds and legacy file extensions, can contain the union of producer-kind matches and untagged extension-fallback matches.

member.name: T:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Extensions.IBlockingDataConsumer
member.summary: Marker interface for a that must consume the data inline, before the call to publish the data returns to the producer.

remarks.para: A regular consumes data asynchronously: the data is queued and processed on a background loop, so there is no guarantee about when runs relative to the producer continuing its work. A consumer that additionally implements is instead invoked inline by the message bus, so the producer's call to publish does not return until has completed. This is useful for extensions that need to guarantee a piece of work happens before the producer proceeds (for example, before a test starts running).

Because consumption happens inline, any exception thrown by propagates back to the producer that published the data, rather than being observed later during drain. Implementations should therefore avoid throwing for non-fatal conditions.

Inline consumption is serialized: only one call runs at a time per consumer. As a consequence, a blocking consumer must not, from within its , publish data that is routed back to itself, as that would deadlock. Note that publishing data where the producer is the consumer itself (same UID) is safe, because the message bus skips delivering a producer's data back to that same producer; the deadlock risk is specifically re-entrant publishing that routes back to this consumer under a different producer UID.
This API is experimental. It may change, break, or be removed at any time without notice.

member.name: P:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Extensions.IExtension.Uid
member.summary: Gets the unique identifier for the extension.
member.remarks:
The value must be a stable string constant that survives class renames. It is SHA-256-hashed for telemetry, displayed verbatim in --info output and error messages, embedded in artifact metadata, and used for feature detection, so changing it silently breaks telemetry continuity and any consumer relying on the previous value.
Do not derive the value from nameof(ImplementingClass): an IDE "Rename Symbol" refactor would then change the UID without any visible diff at the call site. Use an explicit string literal or const instead, even if its initial value happens to match the class name.

member.summary: Property that carries the structured expected and actual values of a failed assertion, so consumers can render an expected-vs-actual diff instead of only a flat failure message.

remarks.para: Historically this information could only travel on under the assert.expected / assert.actual keys. That channel requires the test framework to hand the platform the very exception instance the assertion library threw, which is not always possible: a framework may report a failure without any exception at all (see the overload), or it may only have the message and stack trace as strings once the failure has crossed a process or AppDomain boundary.
Consumers should prefer this property and fall back to the keys for producers that have not been updated yet.

member.name: T:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Extensions.Messages.RetryAttemptProperty
member.summary: Property that identifies a test node update as one attempt of an in-process retry sequence, i.e. several executions of the same test that a test framework performed within a single test host run and reported under the same .
member.remarks:
A test framework that retries a test in-process (for example MSTest's [Retry] attribute) publishes one per attempt, each carrying this property. Consumers that want a single row per test - TRX, JUnit, the process exit code - ignore updates whose is . Consumers that want the whole history - CTRF's retryAttempts[] / flaky, the HTML report, the terminal's retried/flaky counters - keep them all.
This is independent from the out-of-process --retry-failed-tests orchestrator, which re-invokes the whole test host and attributes attempts per host instance instead. When both are in play the two notions compose: the host attempt is the major number and the minor one.

when a later attempt for the same test node follows this one, so this result is not the test's final outcome.

member.name: T:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Extensions.Messages.RetryAttemptPropertyExtensions
member.summary: Helpers for interpreting the in-process retry attribution carried by .
member.remarks: is a sibling of the rather than part of it, mirroring and the output properties: it describes the execution occurrence, not the outcome, and applies to in-progress updates as well as terminal ones. The trade-off is that "is this the test's final outcome?" is not answerable from the state property alone, so every consumer that wants exactly one row per test would otherwise re-implement the same lookup. This helper is that single implementation.

Required and non-empty: it is part of the correlation key, so results from multiple collectors are never silently merged, and it ties a measurement back to its . member.name: T:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Extensions.TestHostControllers.ITestHostControllerConnectionAuthorizer
member.summary: Implemented by an that starts the test host under an operating-system security identity of its own, to authorize that identity on controller-side connections.

remarks.para: The platform protects the controller-to-host connection so that only the account that started the run can use it. On Windows that is the equivalent of PipeOptions.CurrentUserOnly: the pipe is owned by the creating token's owner SID and its access control list grants only that SID.

A launcher that starts the host in a sandbox rather than as a plain child process leaves that host with a different, more restricted identity, which the connection does not yet admit — knowing the connection name is not enough. This interface is how such a launcher declares the identity that must additionally be allowed through.

Controller-side connections must listen before the launcher runs, so a launcher cannot supply the identity from . The platform resolves this interface once before creating those connections, either in controller mode or for an orchestrator such as Retry, and reuses the validated result for the platform connection and controller-side extension pipes. This is why authorization is a separate interface an opts into rather than a member of that interface.

Security. The platform does not grant whatever it is handed. It validates every value and honors only the identity of a single sandboxed application, granting it just the rights required to connect and exchange messages. Anything else — a user, a group, Everyone, or an identity shared by every sandboxed application on the machine — is rejected and fails the run with an actionable error rather than widening the connection. The current-user and elevation protection is always preserved. Returning an empty collection keeps the default behavior exactly as it is.

This is meaningful only where the operating system can express such an identity; today that is Windows, where a sandboxed application is an AppContainer and the values below are its package SID. Elsewhere the returned values are ignored and the connection is created unchanged.
This API is experimental. It may change, break, or be removed at any time without notice.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Extensions.TestHostControllers.ITestHostControllerConnectionAuthorizer.GetAuthorizedSecurityIdentitiesAsync(System.String,System.Threading.CancellationToken)
member.summary: Returns the operating-system security identities that must be able to reach controller-side connections in addition to the current user.
member.remarks: On Windows an identity is a security identifier (SID) in SDDL string form, and only the SID of a single sandboxed application is honored. Return an empty collection when no extra authorization is needed, which is the case for every host started as an ordinary child process and on every operating system that cannot express such an identity.
member.param: The executable path of the test host the platform is about to launch. A package or sandbox can contain several applications with different trust models; implementations should authorize the identity of this selected host, not a sibling application.
member.returns: The security identities to authorize.

member.name: T:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Extensions.TestHostControllers.ITestHostLauncher
member.summary: Allows an extension to control how the out-of-process test host is launched, replacing the platform's default Process.Start behavior.
member.remarks:
The platform keeps owning argument and environment preparation, connection handshakes, lifecycle callbacks, and exit-code reconciliation, and delegates only the single "create and start the test host" step. A controller launch carries the controller IPC/PID handshake; an orchestrator launch can instead carry extension-specific connection metadata such as Retry. Launchers must forward the supplied context opaquely rather than require one specific handshake. The launcher does not have to start a local OS process as long as it returns an the platform can monitor.
This API is experimental. It may change, break, or be removed at any time without notice.

member.name: T:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Extensions.TestHostOrchestrator.ITestHostExecutionOrchestratorMiddleware
member.summary: Represents a single-invocation middleware that composes with other middleware around exactly one existing invocation.

remarks.para: This is a v1, initial composition boundary for test host execution orchestration. Exactly one is still active per run; middleware wraps that single invocation and can only observe or short-circuit it, not replace it with a typed multi-run engine. In particular, this version of the API does not provide repeat/retry-style re-invocation, sharding, phases, protocol metadata, or the ability to mutate identifiers such as attempt number, execution id, or instance id. The existing --retry-failed-tests orchestrator is not reentrant and is not extracted or reimplemented as middleware by this API. A typed, multi-run orchestration model (for example a first-class retry/stress/shard engine) is intentionally out of scope for this version and may be introduced later as a separate, additive capability.

Middleware is composed outermost-first in registration order (see ). This is an explicit, order-dependent composition: there is no numeric ordering key, and middleware must not assume its effect on the pipeline is commutative with other middleware.
This API is experimental. It may change, break, or be removed at any time without notice.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Extensions.TestHostOrchestrator.ITestHostExecutionOrchestratorMiddleware.OrchestrateTestHostExecutionAsync(System.Func{System.Threading.CancellationToken,System.Threading.Tasks.Task{System.Int32}},System.Threading.CancellationToken)
member.summary: Orchestrates test host execution by optionally invoking and returning its result unchanged, or by short-circuiting without invoking at all.

remarks.para: can be invoked at most once, and the call to must begin before this method returns or throws. The platform rejects a second invocation, as well as an invocation deferred until after this method has returned or thrown. Middleware may start the call synchronously and then await its returned task asynchronously, but it cannot defer the call itself to another thread or callback after returning.

When this method invokes and lets it complete (whether or not it also awaits it directly), the value this method returns must be exactly the downstream exit code: this version of the pipeline does not allow middleware to rewrite the downstream verdict. If the downstream execution faults or is canceled, the exception or cancellation must propagate unchanged; converting it to any exit code, including a non-success exit code, is unsupported and rejected by the platform. A downstream failure must not be swallowed into an apparently successful return from this method. When cancellation is signaled anywhere in the linked cancellation chain, the pipeline rethrows the resulting cancellation and does not allow middleware to replace it with a different exit code.

When this method never invokes at all (short-circuiting the pipeline), the returned exit code must not be a success exit code, so that skipped execution can never be reported as if tests actually ran and passed.
The platform links whatever is passed to with the root cancellation token, so passing does not detach the downstream execution from root cancellation.
This API is experimental. It may change, break, or be removed at any time without notice.

member.param: A delegate that invokes the remainder of the pipeline (the next middleware, or the wrapped orchestrator) with the given cancellation token, and returns its exit code.
member.returns: A task representing the asynchronous operation that returns the test host exit code.

member.summary: Executes after the orchestrator runs.
member.remarks: Also invoked when the orchestration was canceled or failed, so that whatever acquired can still be released. Implementations must therefore tolerate being called when their never ran or did not complete, must be safe to call once per run regardless of outcome, and should not assume is still usable — it may already be canceled. Implementations should not throw from this method. When the orchestration was canceled or failed, exceptions thrown from this method are logged and suppressed so they cannot mask the original outcome.
member.param: The exit code of the orchestrator.
member.returns: A task representing the asynchronous operation.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Configurations.AggregatedConfiguration.TryGetCommandLineOptionFromProviders(System.String,System.Boolean@,System.String[]@)
member.summary: Resolves the value of a command-line option across all registered providers at the option granularity (not per-key), so that CLI provider entries fully shadow JSON entries for the same option even when the storage shapes don't overlap (e.g., CLI --list-tests with no args vs. JSON "list-tests": ["json"]).

remarks.para: Providers are walked in registration order; the first one that has any data for wins and its values are returned exclusively. A bare boolean "false" at a winning provider is treated as an explicit disable and short-circuits the search.

Provider contract assumptions for the commandLineOptions:* section (issue #6349):
TryGet returning true with a null value is treated as if the key were absent at this provider — a custom provider that wants to explicitly shadow lower providers must return either the boolean string "False" (disable) or a non-null argument value.
Indexed argument entries are required to be contiguous starting at :0. A gap stops collection — sparse arrays will silently truncate. The JSON provider always emits contiguous indices for arrays.

member.param: Option name with or without leading --.
Set to true if any provider reports the option as set.
Empty for zero-arity / disabled, otherwise the argument list from the winning provider.
member.returns: true if any provider had any data for the option (even an explicit disable); false if no provider mentioned the option.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Configurations.ConfigurationExtensions.IsCommandLineOptionSet(Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Configurations.IConfiguration,System.String)
member.summary: Determines whether the given CLI option name is set, consulting all registered instances (CLI, environment variables, JSON, ...) under the commandLineOptions:* section.

remarks.para: Used by so JSON-sourced options are transparently visible to all consumers (issue #6349).

Resolution is performed at the option granularity by walking the configuration providers in registration order via : the first provider that has any data for the option wins outright and its sibling entries are not merged with later providers. This guarantees that, e.g., an explicit zero-arity --list-tests on the CLI is not silently overridden by an indexed JSON array under the same option.

When the instance is not an (test mocks etc.), falls back to a merged-view lookup via the IConfiguration[key] indexer. In that path the providers cannot be walked, so precedence is per-key rather than per-option.

Note: a JSON bare scalar that happens to be the string "true" or "false" for an option that takes arguments is ambiguous — it is interpreted here as a presence/absence marker rather than as the argument value. Authors should use the array form (["true"], ["false"]) when the literal string is intended.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Configurations.ConfigurationExtensions.TryGetCommandLineOptionArguments(Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Configurations.IConfiguration,System.String,System.String[]@)
member.summary: Returns the argument list for the given CLI option name. Sees values from every registered (CLI, env vars, JSON, ...).

remarks.para: Used by so JSON-sourced options are transparently visible to all consumers (issue #6349).
Resolution mirrors : providers are walked in registration order and the first one with data for the option wins entirely, so CLI/JSON values for the same option never interleave.

Behavior at the winning provider is intentionally a superset of so existing consumers continue to work:
Walks commandLineOptions:<name>:0, :1, ... until a gap is encountered, returning the collected list when non-empty.
Otherwise consults the bare key commandLineOptions:<name>: null => option absent at this provider; a boolean ("true"/"false", case-insensitive) => presence marker (true => set with zero args; false => explicitly not set); any other string => single-element array.

JSON-sourced entries are subject to arity, unknown-option, and per-argument validation in (the validator is given the same JSON view via ), so a JSON typo or bad value fails at startup with the same diagnostics as on the CLI.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Configurations.JsonConfigurationSource.JsonConfigurationProvider.EnumerateCommandLineOptions
member.summary: Enumerates the commandLineOptions section of the loaded testconfig.json file as a list of typed entries, applying the strict schema documented at .

remarks.para:
Supported per-option JSON shapes:
"foo": "bar" — scalar argument (single value).
"foo": true — presence marker, equivalent to --foo on the CLI.
"foo": false — explicit disable; surfaced via .
"foo": ["a", "b"] — multi-value argument list.

Rejected shapes (throw ):
Nested objects like "foo": { "bar": "x" }.
Array of objects like "foo": [ { "bar": "x" } ].
Mixing scalar and indexed entries for the same option name (defensive guard; cannot happen from JSON input but possible if a custom provider mutates the underlying maps).

Empty arrays under commandLineOptions are skipped (treated as absent). Passive defaults reject empty arrays and null values because they must provide at least one argument. This includes a JSON null array element (e.g. "foo": ["a", null]), even inside a mixed array of otherwise-valid scalars. Empty objects are rejected for both sections.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Configurations.JsonConfigurationSource.JsonConfigurationProvider.EnumerateCommandLineOptionDefaults
member.summary: Enumerates passive option argument defaults from the commandLineOptionDefaults section. Scalar booleans are treated as argument values because defaults cannot represent option presence.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Configurations.JsonConfigurationSource.JsonConfigurationProvider.NormalizeCommandLineOptionScalars(System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyDictionary{System.String,Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Extensions.CommandLine.CommandLineOption})
member.summary: Rewrites scalar commandLineOptions:<name> entries to the indexed shape (commandLineOptions:<name>:0) for options registered with >= 1, using as the option registry.

remarks.para: The CLI-backed configuration provider stores zero-arity flags at the bare option key and arg-bearing options under indexed keys (one per argument). The JSON provider cannot distinguish these shapes at parse time because the user freely writes either "foo": "value" (scalar) or "foo": ["value"] (array). For arg-bearing options that always require at least one argument, a scalar value is always the first argument — never a presence marker. Storing it under the indexed key normalizes the shape so both and see one consistent representation.

In particular, this fixes the JSON scalar/bool ambiguity from #6349/#8830: a value like "my-option": "true" for an arg-bearing option used to be misinterpreted as a presence marker (zero arguments) instead of being passed as the first argument value.

Optional-arg options (Min == 0 && Max >= 1) are left untouched because either interpretation (presence vs. scalar argument) is semantically valid; users who need to disambiguate should use the explicit array form.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Configurations.JsonConfigurationSource.JsonConfigurationProvider.GetSection(System.String)
member.summary: Returns the immediate (one-level) string entries under from the loaded JSON configuration file.
member.remarks:
The method enforces a strict schema for the section:
The section value must be a JSON object (not a scalar, an array, etc.).
Each direct child must be a scalar (string/number/bool/null) — the parser converts non-strings to text.
Nested objects or arrays are rejected; an explicit empty object/array entry is also rejected.
Throws with a descriptive message (including the configuration file path) when the schema is violated.

member.name: F:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.DynamicExtensions.DynamicExtensionConstants.PathComparison
member.summary: How two file paths are compared. Windows paths are case-insensitive, other platforms' are not, and using a single comparison everywhere keeps de-duplication and the load-context cache in agreement.
member.remarks: This keys off the OS rather than the actual volume, which is an approximation: a default macOS volume is case-insensitive, and a Linux or macOS volume can be either. The approximation is deliberately biased toward the visible failure. Treating a case-insensitive volume as case-sensitive means two manifests that spell the same file differently register it twice — which the run then lists on its output, so it can be seen and fixed. The opposite bias would silently drop one of two genuinely distinct extensions, which is the failure mode this design exists to avoid. Resolving it properly needs canonical file identity rather than a path comparison, which is not worth a syscall per resolved assembly here.

member.name: F:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.DynamicExtensions.DynamicExtensionConstants.SharedContractAssemblyNames
member.summary: Simple names of the assemblies that are always resolved from the default load context, so that the platform contract types have a single identity shared between the host and every dynamically loaded extension.

remarks.para: Microsoft.Testing.Platform is the core contract: without it the ITestApplicationBuilder an extension sees would be a different type from the one the platform passes to it.

The remaining entries are the first-party *.Abstractions assemblies whose types are *exchanged* between extensions — for example ITrxReportCapability, which one extension implements and another queries for. Sharing them by name rather than relying on whether the file happens to sit next to the extension keeps identity deterministic instead of dependent on the deployment layout.

Anything not listed here is isolated. Add to this list only assemblies that carry types crossing the host/extension boundary; adding an implementation assembly would reintroduce the dependency conflicts this design exists to avoid.

member.name: T:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Helpers.ObjectPool`1
member.summary:
Generic implementation of object pooling pattern with predefined pool size limit. The main purpose is that limited number of frequently used objects can be kept in the pool for further recycling.
Notes: 1) it is not the goal to keep all returned objects. Pool is not meant for storage. If there is no space in the pool, extra returned objects will be dropped.
2) it is implied that if object was obtained from a pool, the caller will return it back in a relatively short time. Keeping checked out objects for long durations is ok, but reduces usefulness of pooling. Just new up your own.
Not returning objects to the pool in not detrimental to the pool's work, but is a bad practice. Rationale: If there is no intent for reusing the object, do not use pool - just use "new".

member.name: T:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Helpers.RuntimeFeatureHelper
member.summary: Runtime feature detection that the platform uses to adapt its behavior to the host.

member.name: P:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Helpers.RuntimeFeatureHelper.IsMultiThreaded
member.summary: Gets a value indicating whether the current runtime supports multiple threads.
member.remarks:
Single-threaded WebAssembly runtimes (browser-wasm and wasi-wasm) do not have a thread pool: Task.Run continuations never execute while the single thread is busy, and blocking waits (Task.Wait / GetAwaiter().GetResult() on an incomplete task) throw . Code that would otherwise offload work to a background thread MUST fall back to inline/synchronous execution when this returns , otherwise the operation deadlocks or throws.
This is the single condition to branch on before calling ITask.RunLongRunning, creating a , or using a blocking primitive such as BlockingCollection<T>. Do not hand-roll an equivalent probe at the call site. There are two established fallbacks, and which one applies depends on whether the work is observable:
Best-effort background diagnostics (shutdown watchdog, slow-test reporters) are simply skipped. Scheduling them with Task.Run instead would not help: the loop would not run while the single thread is busy, and awaiting it during teardown would hang.
Work whose result is observable (the TRX streaming store's sidecar writer) is restructured to run inline on the calling thread. Note that swapping the producer/consumer hand-off for Task.Run is not sufficient on its own when the loop body blocks — the blocking wait has to be removed as well.
.NET 11 exposes System.Runtime.CompilerServices.RuntimeFeature.IsMultithreadingSupported for exactly this purpose (approved and implemented via ), and it is additionally a trimming feature switch, so it can light up dead-code elimination. The platform still targets earlier frameworks, so we derive the same information from the single-threaded-wasm probes, which are available since .NET 8. Once net11.0 is in SupportedNetFrameworks this property should forward to the BCL API under a #if NET11_0_OR_GREATER.

member.name: T:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.IPC.NamedPipeServerSecurity
member.summary: Windows-only helpers that create a controller named pipe whose discretionary access control list (DACL) keeps the current-user protection of PipeOptions.CurrentUserOnly while additionally authorizing a small, explicitly requested set of AppContainer package SIDs.

remarks.para: Why this exists. On Windows, .NET implements PipeOptions.CurrentUserOnly with a security descriptor whose owner is the creating token's owner SID and whose DACL contains a single ACE granting that same SID full control. An AppContainer (UWP, or a WinUI app configured for AppContainer) runs with a restricted token: Windows performs the normal access check against the token's user/group SIDs and a second check against the token's restricting SIDs, which for an AppContainer contain the package SID. Access is granted only when both checks succeed, so a DACL that names only the user SID denies the AppContainer client even though it belongs to the same signed-in user. Knowing the pipe name is therefore not enough — the package SID must appear in the DACL. See https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/secauthz/restricted-tokens.
Security model. The descriptor produced here is deliberately minimal and fully explicit:

list.item: Owner and group are the current token's owner SID, exactly like PipeOptions.CurrentUserOnly. This preserves the elevation split (an elevated token's owner is BUILTIN\Administrators, a non-elevated one's is the user) and keeps the client-side PipeOptions.CurrentUserOnly owner validation working.
The DACL is protected (P), so no inherited ACE can widen it.
The owner SID gets FILE_ALL_ACCESS-equivalent rights (the same mask .NET grants).

Every authorized package SID gets only — read, write, read the security descriptor (needed by the client-side owner validation) and synchronize. Notably it does not include FILE_CREATE_PIPE_INSTANCE, so an authorized package can never create another instance of the pipe and impersonate the controller.

Only genuine AppContainer SIDs may be authorized (see ). The catch-all ALL APPLICATION PACKAGES / ALL RESTRICTED APPLICATION PACKAGES SIDs, user SIDs, group SIDs and Everyone are rejected by construction, so the extension point that feeds this type can only ever widen access to one specific packaged application.
The pipe additionally rejects remote clients (PIPE_REJECT_REMOTE_CLIENTS), which the default .NET pipe does not do.

No mandatory integrity label is emitted, so the pipe keeps the controller's own integrity level and Mandatory Integrity Control remains a second gate behind the DACL. An AppContainer client is admitted by its package-SID ACE alone.

remarks.para: The implementation goes through CreateNamedPipeW rather than PipeSecurity because the managed ACL types are not part of the netstandard2.0 surface this assembly also builds for, and because PipeOptions.CurrentUserOnly cannot be combined with an explicit descriptor.

member.name: F:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Logging.FileLogger.MaxLogFileCreationAttempts
member.summary: Number of attempts made to create the diagnostic log file before giving up. Every candidate after the first carries the current process id and a process-wide counter, so candidates are unique across every logger in this process and against any other process racing on the same log folder: a collision can therefore only ever happen on the first attempt. Bounding by attempts rather than by elapsed wall-clock time keeps the loop provably terminating and immune to a stalled or forward-jumping clock ( is wall time, not monotonic). FileLoggerTests mirrors this value; keep the two in sync.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Messages.ShutdownTimeouts.GetCanceledConsumerCompletion(Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Helpers.IEnvironment)
member.summary: Gets the budget for completing the consumer handshake once the run has already been canceled. It bounds the shutdown as a whole rather than each consumer: completes its processors sequentially, so a per-consumer budget would let N uncooperative consumers multiply it. Can be overridden through .
member.remarks: Only the canceled path is bounded. On a normal run the wait stays unbounded, because a consumer that legitimately takes a long time to flush its final results (a large TRX or coverage report) must not be cut off. On an aborted run the trade-off flips: a cooperative consumer unwinds as soon as it observes the cancellation token, so anything still running after this budget is ignoring the token, and letting it block the abort indefinitely would hang the cancellations that have no second escape hatch ('--timeout', '--maximum-failed-tests'), unlike an interactive Ctrl+C which can be pressed again.

member.name: T:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.DotnetTestPassthroughOutputDevice
member.summary:
The host output device used under the dotnet test pipe protocol. Like it discards regular (informational) host output (the SDK's TerminalTestReporter owns user-facing rendering), but it additionally forwards three classes of host message to the SDK over the pipe so they are not swallowed in multi-assembly runs:
is forwarded as an informational so durable framework and extension messages reach the SDK-owned terminal reporter (protocol 1.3.0+).
Lines marked with are forwarded verbatim as so the AzureDevOpsReport extension's logging commands (##[group], ##vso[...]) still reach the pipeline log (protocol 1.2.0+, only on an Azure DevOps agent where the extension produces them).
and are forwarded as so host-side diagnostics produced outside test results (hang/crash dump diagnostics, retry summaries, generic extension/framework warnings and errors) reach the SDK, which routes them to its TerminalTestReporter's WriteWarningMessage / WriteErrorMessage (protocol 1.3.0+).
member.remarks: Forwarding is gated on the SDK negotiating the relevant protocol version ( for Azure DevOps commands, for display messages); against an older SDK the corresponding lines are swallowed exactly like the no-op device, so no unknown message id is ever sent. Plain informational output ( / ) is still discarded; only explicitly durable session messages, warnings, and errors cross the wire. The and the dotnet test execution id are resolved lazily because both become available only after the output device is built (the connection is created and the execution id env var is set during AfterCommonServiceSetupAsync).

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.TerminalOutputDevice.IsRetryAttemptAfterTheFirst(Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Helpers.IEnvironment)
member.summary: Returns whether this process is a retry attempt of a --retry-failed-tests run, that is the second or a later one. The retry orchestrator stamps the 1-based attempt number on every test host it launches, so anything above 1 re-runs only the tests that failed previously. Such an attempt must not print a run summary: its counts describe that filtered subset, not the run, and the orchestrator reconciles every attempt into a single retry summary at the end. The first attempt executes the whole suite, so its summary is accurate and is left alone — as is every run that is not orchestrated at all.

redraws the progress block in place on every refresh tick (used for cursor-capable ANSI terminals).

member.name: T:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.TerminalTestReporter
member.summary: Terminal test reporter that outputs test progress and is capable of writing ANSI or non-ANSI output via the given terminal.
member.remarks: The implementation is split across partials named for what they render or track: Lifecycle (run and assembly start/stop), Messaging (progress messages and in-progress tests), TestCompletion and TestDiscovery (per-test execution and discovery output), Handshake and ErroredAssemblies (orchestrator-only failure recaps, each owning its own record list), Summary (the post-run verdict and counter lines), FlakyTests, SlowestTests and Coverage (the sections appended below that summary), and Formatting plus Formatting.ControlCharacters (exceptions, stack traces, assembly links, durations and control-character escaping). This file holds the core shared state, the constants, construction and the collected artifacts.

member.summary: The two directory separator characters to be passed to methods like .

member.name: F:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.TerminalTestReporter._assemblies
member.summary: Per-assembly run state, keyed by the caller-provided execution id. The in-process Microsoft.Testing.Platform host registers a single assembly; the dotnet test orchestrator registers one entry per child test assembly. Progress rendering already supports N workers (slots), so this only generalizes the bookkeeping.

member.name: F:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.TerminalTestReporter._erroredAssemblies
member.summary: Assemblies that handshaked but then exited with a non-zero code without reporting any failed test (crash, Environment.FailFast, a hang-dump kill, an option rejected after the handshake, ...). Their process output is printed inline when the assembly completes, but in a large multi-assembly run that inline output is scrolled far above the summary, so we also record it here and re-print it in an end-of-run recap.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.TerminalTestReporter.RecordErroredAssembly(Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.TestProgressState,System.Int32,System.String,System.String)
member.summary: Records an assembly that ended unsuccessfully with no failed test so its process output (exit code + stdout + stderr) can be re-printed at the end of the run. Orchestrator-only: only the multi-process dotnet test orchestrator reaches the exit-code overload of .

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.TerminalTestReporter.AppendErroredAssemblyRecap(Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.ITerminal)
member.summary: Re-print assemblies that errored during the run (non-zero exit with no failed test) so that — as with the handshake-failure recap — the actionable process output is shown at the end of the run rather than buried in the middle of a large multi-assembly run.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.TerminalTestReporter.AppendFlakyTests(Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.ITerminal,System.Collections.Generic.List{Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.TestProgressState})
member.summary: Appends the "Flaky tests" section listing, by name, the tests that failed at least once but whose final attempt passed. Retried tests that never recovered are deliberately not listed: they are already reported as failures with their full error output, so a second listing would only duplicate. For a single assembly a flat list is rendered; the multi-assembly orchestrator groups per assembly. No-op when the feature is off or when no test was flaky.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.TerminalTestReporter.AppendLongDuration(Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.ITerminal,System.TimeSpan,System.Boolean,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Appends a long duration in human readable format such as 1h 23m 500ms.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.TerminalTestReporter.AppendAssemblySummary(Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.TestProgressState,Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.ITerminal)
member.summary: Renders the per-assembly summary line (link + result + compact counts + duration). Used by the dotnet test orchestrator (); the in-process host renders a single run-level summary instead.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.TerminalTestReporter.AppendAssemblyTestCounts(Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.ITerminal,Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.TestProgressState)
member.summary: Renders a compact, per-assembly counts block that mirrors the in-progress indicator. Full-ANSI terminals get "[✓P/xF/↓S]" (with optional "/rR"); simple terminals (NoAnsi / SimpleAnsi / CI) get the ASCII "[+P/xF/?S]" form so logs stay font- and encoding-friendly.

member.name: P:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.TerminalTestReporter.HasHandshakeFailure
member.summary: Gets a value indicating whether any assembly failed to handshake (e.g. a child test host process exited before it could start a session). Used by the dotnet test orchestrator to surface a non-success exit even when no test result was ever reported.

member.name: P:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.TerminalTestReporter.HandshakeFailureCount
member.summary: Gets the number of assemblies that failed to handshake. Counted toward the run summary's "error" line.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.TerminalTestReporter.HandshakeFailure(System.String,System.String,System.Int32,System.String,System.String,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Report that an assembly failed to produce a usable handshake. This is an orchestrator-only path (the in-process host always handshakes); it records the failure so flips and the failure is re-printed in the end-of-run recap, and prints the immediate failure context.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.TerminalTestReporter.AppendHandshakeFailureRecap(Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.ITerminal)
member.summary: Re-print handshake failures captured during the run so that — even when there is a lot of diagnostic output before the summary — the user sees the actionable failure context (assembly, exit code, stdout, stderr) at the end of the run rather than having to scroll back.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.TerminalTestReporter.AssemblyRunCompleted(System.String,System.Int32,System.String,System.String)
member.summary: Orchestrator overload: completes an assembly run with the child process exit code and captured output. When the was never registered (the process exited before a usable handshake), the completion is surfaced as a rather than throwing. On a non-zero exit code the executable summary (exit code + stdout/stderr) is printed.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.TerminalTestReporter.TestInProgress(System.String,System.String,System.String,System.String,System.String,System.String,System.String)
member.summary: Orchestrator overload (dotnet test): carries the assembly/target-framework/architecture and per-attempt instance id known to the multi-process orchestrator. The shared in-progress tracking is keyed by execution id, so those extra arguments are accepted for signature parity and the overload delegates to the core method.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.TerminalTestReporter.AppendSlowestTests(Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.ITerminal,System.Collections.Generic.List{Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.TestProgressState})
member.summary: Appends the opt-in "Slowest tests" section, ranking the longest-running tests by their reported execution duration. For a single assembly a flat list is rendered; for the multi-assembly orchestrator each assembly gets its own sub-list so the ranking stays scoped per assembly. No-op when the feature is off or when no timed tests were recorded.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.TerminalTestReporter.AppendRetrySummaryLines(Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.ITerminal,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: Appends the retry accounting lines that sit between the skipped count and the duration: flaky: N (tests that failed at least once but eventually passed) and retried: N tests, M extra runs. Both are omitted entirely when nothing was retried, so a run without retries keeps its historical summary byte-for-byte.

In-process host overload carrying the in-process retry attribution of the result. Passing the itself rather than its parts keeps the three facts it carries - the attempt number, that the result belongs to a retry sequence at all, and whether a later attempt supersedes it - together, so a caller cannot forward some and drop the rest. A framework that does not retry passes .

Orchestrator overload (dotnet test): carries the assembly/target-framework/architecture and the per-attempt instance id that the multi-process orchestrator knows. The instance id drives retry attribution in ; assembly/tfm/arch are accepted for signature parity and the future per-test assembly link.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.TerminalTestReporter.IsTestResultVisible(Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.TestOutcome)
member.summary: Determines whether a completed test's per-test terminal block (result line, informative details, stack trace, expected/actual, and captured stdout/stderr) should be rendered, based on . , , , and are all gated by : they render identically (see ) and are indistinguishable to a user deciding what to see.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.TerminalTestReporter.TestDiscovered(System.String,System.String,System.String,System.String,System.Nullable{System.Int32})
member.summary: Orchestrator overload (dotnet test): the multi-process orchestrator also knows each discovered test's uid, file path and line number. The shared discovery summary currently lists display names only, so those are accepted for signature parity. When is missing the is used as the listed name; when neither is available the test is still counted (so the discovery total stays correct) but no blank entry is added to the summary.

member.summary: Resolves --show-flaky-tests. See .

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.TerminalTestReporterCommandLineOptionsProvider.GetShowTestResultsVisibility(Microsoft.Testing.Platform.CommandLine.ICommandLineOptions)
member.summary: Resolves --show-test-results or its passive configuration default, returning when neither is present so the caller (TerminalOutputDevice.InitializeAsync) can fall back to its --output-based default. Arguments are already guaranteed valid by by the time a real run reaches this method; an unexpected parse failure therefore indicates that command-line validation was bypassed and is reported as an invalid application state.

member.summary: Parses the raw --show-test-results arguments (as aggregated across every occurrence of the option and every space-separated token within each occurrence) into a flag set. Each raw token is additionally split on , so passed,skipped, passed skipped, and --show-test-results passed --show-test-results skipped are all equivalent. Values are matched case-insensitively and the ordinary values (passed/failed/skipped) are unioned and de-duplicated. all and none are each rejected when combined with any other value (including each other), and an entirely empty selection (e.g. a lone comma) is rejected too.

member.summary: Gets a value indicating whether tests that failed at least once but eventually passed after a retry are reported (the "flaky: N" summary line and the "Flaky tests" section). On by default; turned off by --show-flaky-tests off. Has no effect on a run where nothing was retried.

member.name: P:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.Terminal.TerminalTestReporterOptions.ShowRunSummary
member.summary: Gets a value indicating whether the run-summary verdict and its counts are rendered. Turned off for the retry attempts of the --retry-failed-tests orchestrator, meaning the second and later ones: those re-run only the previously-failed tests, so their summary reports a shrinking, filtered subset ("total: 1" for a four-test suite) that reads as the run's verdict but is not. The first attempt executes the whole suite, so its summary is accurate and is kept. The orchestrator then prints one reconciled retry summary at the end. Everything else — produced artifacts, the slowest-tests section and the error recaps — is still rendered for every attempt, since none of it is restated by the orchestrator.

member.summary: Returns a snapshot of currently running tasks, sorted by elapsed time descending and truncated to entries (the last entry becomes a "... N more running" summary detail when truncation occurs).
member.remarks: The returned is a cached buffer reused across calls on the same instance to avoid per-render-tick allocation. Callers MUST NOT call on the same instance again before finishing use of the previously-returned buffer — the next call on that instance will and rebuild it in place, silently invalidating the prior caller's view. Buffers from different instances are independent and may be held concurrently. This type is not designed for concurrent calls on the same instance; the production caller (AnsiTerminalTestProgressFrame) only invokes this from the single-threaded render loop.

member.summary: Shared helper for computing test run verdicts and formatting plain-text summaries. Used by both (verdict logic) and (full plain-text summary).

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.TestRunSummaryHelper.IsRunFailed(System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Boolean,System.Int32,Microsoft.Testing.Platform.CommandLine.ZeroTestsPolicy)
member.summary: Determines whether the test run should be considered failed based on the given outcome counters and state.
member.remarks: controls whether an all-skipped run is treated as a failed "zero tests" run. Under (the default) only a run that discovered no test at all fails as zero tests; under skipped tests don't count as run, so an all-skipped run also fails. A run where no test was found is always treated as failed regardless of policy.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.OutputDevice.TestRunSummaryHelper.GetVerdictText(System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Boolean,System.Int32,System.Boolean,System.Boolean,Microsoft.Testing.Platform.CommandLine.ZeroTestsPolicy)
member.summary: Computes the verdict string for the test run.
member.remarks:
The two orchestrator-only flags surface non-test failures that must not be masked by the test-count wording:
: at least one assembly failed to hand-shake. This escalates to "Failed!" ahead of the "Zero tests ran" branch (a handshake failure is not a benign empty run).
: at least one assembly process ended unsuccessfully (e.g. crashed or returned a non-zero exit code) even though its tests passed. This escalates the verdict wording to "Failed!" but only AFTER the "Zero tests ran" branch, so a project that legitimately contains zero tests (which exits non-zero by design) keeps the "Zero tests ran" wording rather than "Failed!". Note this only affects the displayed verdict text: still treats a zero-test run as a failed run.
In-process callers never have either condition and pass , so their verdict is unchanged. mirrors : under (the default) an all-skipped run is reported as "Passed!" instead of "Zero tests ran". Under an all-skipped run is reported as "Zero tests ran".

The current grammar for the filter looks as follows:
TREE_NODE_FILTER = EXPR ( '/' EXPR )* EXPR = '(' EXPR ')' | EXPR OP EXPR | NODE_VALUE FILTER_EXPR = '(' FILTER_EXPR ')' | TOKEN '=' TOKEN | TOKEN '!=' TOKEN | FILTER_EXPR OP FILTER_EXPR | TOKEN OP = '&' | '|' NODE_VALUE = TOKEN | TOKEN '[' FILTER_EXPR ']' TOKEN = string
OR expressions are supported for a single path segment, for example: /A/B/C/(Test1|Test2).
OR expressions over full paths are not supported, for example: (/A/B/C/Test1)|(/A/B/C/Test2).
member.exception: Exception thrown, if the filter is malformed, for example A(|B) or A).

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.DotnetTestConnection.StartServerControlChannelAsync(System.Func{System.Threading.CancellationToken,System.Threading.Tasks.Task})
member.summary: Opens the reverse "server control" pipe the SDK advertised during the handshake and parks a long-poll on it. The SDK completes that request with a whenever it wants to signal the test host (today only ). On cancel - or when the control pipe drops, which means the host went away - is invoked exactly once so the caller can stop the run cooperatively (preferring a graceful stop so trx/artifacts are still produced).
member.param: The reaction to a server-initiated cancel. It receives the test application cancellation token.
member.remarks: Both the connect and the long-poll run entirely on a background task, so test start is never blocked on this auxiliary channel. This is best-effort: if the control pipe cannot be established the test run continues unaffected (the feature simply stays off). Callers should only invoke this after a successful handshake and when is . It is invoked once per connection on the awaited run path (before the test run starts), so the control-channel fields below are written here and only read later during exit/dispose - the single-threaded lifecycle makes the plain fields safe without extra synchronization.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.ServerMode.TcpMessageHandler.ReadHeaderLineAsync(System.Threading.CancellationToken)
member.summary: Reads a single CRLF-terminated header line from the shared byte buffer. Headers are ASCII by protocol, but they are decoded as UTF-8 (a superset) so a non-conformant peer cannot corrupt the framing. Returns at end of stream.
member.remarks: Only LF terminates a line here. The this replaced also treated a lone CR as a terminator; the protocol always sends CRLF, so dropping that is deliberate and keeps a CR inside a header value from splitting the line.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.ServerMode.TcpMessageHandler.TrimPreamble(System.String)
member.summary: Drops a UTF-8 byte-order mark from the very first line of the stream. The previous -based reader had byte-order-mark detection enabled by default and silently swallowed the preamble, so peers that write their headers through a preamble-emitting encoder (for example new StreamWriter(stream, Encoding.UTF8)) kept working. Preserve that tolerance.

member.name: T:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Services.IClientCapabilities
member.summary: Represents the capabilities declared by the client that is driving the test host.
member.remarks:
Capabilities are opt-in: unless a client explicitly declares a capability, the platform assumes the most conservative (default) behavior. Use when the distinction between an explicitly stateless client and an undeclared capability is required.
This API is experimental. It may change, break, or be removed at any time without notice.

member.name: P:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Services.IClientCapabilities.IsStateful
member.summary: Gets a value indicating whether the client is stateful.
member.remarks: A stateful client persists an addressable set of test nodes for the whole session and keeps each node in its last-known state until it is explicitly updated (for example, an IDE test explorer). A stateless client consumes updates as a stream and does not retain node state after the run (for example, dotnet test). The default is (stateless); a client opts into stateful behavior. This capability is independent of connection lifetime and multi-request support.

member.name: T:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Telemetry.EnvironmentTraceContext
member.summary: Reads a W3C trace context from the environment so that a test run started by an already-traced parent (a CI pipeline step, dotnet test, an IDE, or a test host controller) nests under that parent instead of starting an orphan trace.
member.remarks: The TRACEPARENT / TRACESTATE environment variables are the de-facto standard used by the OpenTelemetry ecosystem (and by build systems such as Azure Pipelines and GitHub Actions runners that expose them for child processes). We deliberately only read them: exporting the current context to child processes is done separately by the test host controller.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Telemetry.EnvironmentTraceContext.IsValidTraceParent(System.String)
member.summary: Validates the version-traceid-spanid-flags shape, so a malformed variable in the environment cannot poison the whole trace.
member.remarks: The rules mirror what System.Diagnostics enforces internally, because when it rejects a parent id it does so silently and starts a brand new trace instead - which is exactly the hard-to-debug outcome this validation exists to turn into a clean "no parent". In particular the hex digits must be lowercase and the version must not be ff.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Telemetry.IPlatformOpenTelemetryService.StartActivity(System.String,System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable{System.Collections.Generic.KeyValuePair{System.String,System.Object}},System.String,System.DateTimeOffset)
member.summary: Starts an activity.
member.remarks: Do not change this signature. Extensions ship independently of the platform, and the C# compiler bakes optional-parameter defaults into the call site, so an already-published extension binary references this exact signature. Adding a parameter here - even an optional one - removes that signature and makes the older extension fail with a MissingMethodException at run time. Add a new method instead, and note that no analyzer catches this: it only shows up in the forward-compatibility acceptance test.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Telemetry.IPlatformOpenTelemetryService.StartNonAmbientActivity(System.String,System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable{System.Collections.Generic.KeyValuePair{System.String,System.Object}},System.String)
member.summary: Starts an activity that is timed and exported but never becomes the ambient activity.
member.remarks:
This matters for code that captures an while the span is open: the ambient activity is an async-local, so it would be captured too and later restored - parenting unrelated, much later work to a span that has already ended. MSTest does exactly that when it propagates async-locals set by AssemblyInitialize/ClassInitialize to every subsequent test.
When is omitted, the span inherits the current ambient activity as its parent without replacing that activity as current. Pass to select a different parent explicitly.
member.param: Attributes to set on the span at creation time.
The explicit parent of the span, or to inherit the current ambient activity.

member.name: M:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Telemetry.OpenTelemetryResultHandler.GetFullyQualifiedName(Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Extensions.Messages.TestMethodIdentifierProperty)
member.summary: Builds the value for code.function.name, which the convention defines as the fully qualified name.

remarks.para: A type in the global namespace contributes no namespace segment, so the name must not gain a leading dot. Two spellings have to be recognised, because the property is a plain string filled in by whichever test framework produced the node: an empty namespace (what MSTest produces, since it derives the namespace by splitting the managed type name) and Roslyn's <global namespace>, which is what INamespaceSymbol.ToDisplayString() returns when the caller does not first check IsGlobalNamespace.

Dropping the segment - rather than emitting Roslyn's global:: prefix - keeps the attribute language-agnostic, matches the convention's own examples, and is consistent with how the rest of this repository treats the global namespace (see TestClassModelBuilder, ReflectionMetadataGenerator and DiscoveredTestsJsonSerializer, which all omit it).

member.name: T:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Telemetry.TestingPlatformSemanticConventions
member.summary: Well-known attribute and instrument names emitted by Microsoft.Testing.Platform.

remarks.para: Where an OpenTelemetry semantic convention exists, its exact name is used: test.*, code.*, error.*, cicd.*, vcs.*, host.*, os.* and process.*. Several of those are still at "development" or "release candidate" stability upstream, so keeping every name in one file means a rename upstream is a single-file change here.

Names marked "platform extension" below have no upstream definition as of semantic conventions 1.43.0 - notably there are no upstream test.* metrics at all, and no upstream span conventions for test cases. They deliberately sit in the test.* namespace because that is where an upstream definition would land, and they are documented as ours rather than presented as standard.

member.name: T:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.TestHostOrchestrator.TestHostExecutionOrchestratorMiddlewarePipeline
member.summary: Builds and runs the guarded, single-invocation chain wrapped around one invocation. See for the contract middleware must follow and for the v1 scope boundary (single-invocation composition around exactly one orchestrator; no repeat, sharding, phases, or protocol metadata).
member.remarks: All pipeline state (in-flight downstream tasks, per-frame single-invocation guards) is local to one call: nothing is shared or reused across separate runs.

member.name: T:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.TestHostOrchestrator.TestHostExecutionOrchestratorMiddlewarePipeline.SingleInvocationNext
member.summary: Guards a single next() continuation and, once accepted, owns the lifecycle of whatever downstream that invocation produces.

remarks.para: is preallocated in the constructor - strictly before this guard is ever handed to a middleware - so it is always a real, non-null, awaitable from the very first instant any other thread could observe as . This also makes the accepted downstream task safe to await while the synchronous prefix of inner() is still running. The middleware contract requires the call to next() itself to begin before the middleware returns or throws; only the returned task may be observed asynchronously after that point.

Lock invariant. Acceptance (the "single invocation" state transition from open to invoked), registration of into the shared in-flight drain list, and (the transition from open to closed once a frame stops accepting new invocations) are all performed while holding the exact same inFlightLock object that
holds when it reads that list. This closes an otherwise-real gap: accepting an invocation (deciding it should run) and registering it for draining used to be two separate steps - a lock-free state transition immediately followed by a separately-locked list append - so an invocation that had already begun while its middleware was returning or throwing could race the drain: the state transition could have already succeeded (so the invocation is "accepted" and cannot be rejected later) while the corresponding list append had not yet happened, letting a concurrently-running top-level drain miss it entirely and let the whole pipeline report completion while that still-accepted invocation (and whatever it eventually starts, up to and including the wrapped orchestrator) keeps running unmanaged underneath. Folding accept-and-register into one critical section - guarded by the very same lock the drain uses - makes that outcome impossible: by construction, any accepted invocation is present before the lock is released, and the drain keeps consuming newly appended descendants until the list is exhausted. Symmetrically, once has run (always synchronously, in the owning frame's own finally, before that frame's own exception or return value can propagate any further), any later call to observes the frame already closed under that same lock and is rejected outright - it can never proceed to call inner() at all, so there is nothing from a rejected call that could ever need draining.

Only the state check/transition and the list mutation happen under the lock; everything else - linked-token-source creation, the actual call into inner() (arbitrary extension or leaf code, which may itself block synchronously for an arbitrary duration), and publishing the outcome - runs outside it, so the lock is held only briefly and user code never runs while any other frame is blocked waiting for it (including the drain snapshot).

member.name: P:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.TestHostOrchestrator.TestHostExecutionOrchestratorMiddlewarePipeline.SingleInvocationNext.DownstreamTask
member.summary: Gets the downstream task. Always non-null (see the type-level remarks). Only ever awaited once is observed - an uninvoked guard's placeholder is simply left pending forever and garbage-collected along with this guard, never awaited by anything, so it can never hang the pipeline or leak.

member.name: P:Microsoft.Testing.Platform.TestHostOrchestrator.TestHostExecutionOrchestratorMiddlewarePipeline.SingleInvocationNext.EffectiveToken
member.summary: Gets the actual composite token passed to the wrapped continuation once has run. Linked from every ancestor in the chain (the ambient token, which already carries root plus every outer middleware's own child token by induction), the absolute root token (linked again explicitly as a hard, chain-independent guarantee), and whatever token this frame's middleware itself passed to next. Only ever read after has already completed (see ), by which point it is guaranteed to already hold its final value - see the type-level remarks on publication ordering.

member.name: T:System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.DynamicallyAccessedMembersAttribute
member.summary: Indicates that certain members on a specified are accessed dynamically, for example through .
member.remarks:
This allows tools to understand which members are being accessed during the execution of a program.
This attribute is valid on members whose type is or .
When this attribute is applied to a location of type , the assumption is that the string represents a fully qualified type name.
When this attribute is applied to a class, interface, or struct, the members specified can be accessed dynamically on instances returned from calling on instances of that class, interface, or struct.
If the attribute is applied to a method it's treated as a special case and it implies the attribute should be applied to the "this" parameter of the method. As such the attribute should only be used on instance methods of types assignable to System.Type (or string, but no methods will use it there).
